title: Morocco and North African music
summary: Moore recalls Casablanca and Meknes, a North African singer, and Arabic music.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: How was it in North Africa?

In North Africa? Our first engagement was in Casablanca and it seemed to me American jazz was very great over there because our group and Mezz Mezzrow's group and at one time, in Meknes, I think it was, I saw an ad for a singer that was going to perform at one of the Moroccan theaters and although I don't speak any Morocco or French, I went to the theater just for curiosity, I paid my francs or whatever their change money and I didn't want to sit down, and the show came

on and this fella, he was like the Frank Sinatra of North Africa. I could see why he was popular from the way he did his songs.

No, I don't remember the name but he was pretty famous. That was quite an experience just listening to the young man, especially when he was coming out of a song. His voice, the way he carried his voice up and down the register, he had a particular way of -- with North African songs.
Oh, yes, the way that they have a way of quavering a voice, using kind of a shaking.
You could just about tell when they were going to end --

That's it, that's Arabic tunes. And it always knocks me out to listen to other music because if you're walking along the streets in Morocco, I'd listen to the string music of the Arabs. It would knock me out, and then -- I think there's places there where you can buy tea, their tea tastes like roots. They have a different type of tea.
They have their mint tea and so forth.
Mint flavor -- mint. Oh, Moroccan teas are beautiful.

There are musicians that play those oboe-like instruments called the alghaita. and they really get a big sound out of that instrument. You've heard them, I'm sure.
Oh, yea, I was interested in everything, when I was sitting in that theater, you know.
